\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{おたま} (otama)}{おたま (otama)}]{\ja{おたま} (otama) — a ladle}

\label{lesson:JA-C103-otama}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a rice pot, then the Japanese for a chopping board.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{おたま}}
\textbf{\ja{おたま}} — \emph{otama} — \textquotedblleft{}a ladle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{おたま}} (\emph{otama}) is native: the polite \emph{o-} and \emph{tama}, \textquotedblleft{}ball\textquotedblright{}, the ladle's round bowl. JMdict marks it as a shortened word. It is inherited rather than borrowed.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{すいどう} (suidou)}{すいどう (suidou)}]{\ja{すいどう} (suidou) — the water supply}

\label{lesson:JA-C103-suidou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a chopping board, then the Japanese for a ladle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{すいどう}}
\textbf{\ja{すいどう}} — \emph{suidou} — \textquotedblleft{}the water supply\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{すいどう}} (\emph{suidou}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{sui}, \textquotedblleft{}water\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{sywijX}) and \emph{dō}, \textquotedblleft{}way, path\textquotedblright{} (\emph{dawX}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{やかん} (yakan)}{やかん (yakan)}]{\ja{やかん} (yakan) — a kettle}

\label{lesson:JA-C103-yakan}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a ladle, then the Japanese for the water supply.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{やかん}}
\textbf{\ja{やかん}} — \emph{yakan} — \textquotedblleft{}a kettle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{やかん}} (\emph{yakan}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{yaku}, \textquotedblleft{}medicine\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{yak}) and \emph{kan}, \textquotedblleft{}jar\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kwanH}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese after Baxter–Sagart). It was a pot for brewing medicine, and \emph{yaku} shortened to \emph{ya}; JMdict marks it as usually written in kana.
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{かん} (kan)}{かん (kan)}]{\ja{かん} (kan) — a can, a tin}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{かん}}
\textbf{\ja{かん}} — \emph{kan} — \textquotedblleft{}a can, a tin\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{かん}} (\emph{kan}) is a loanword: JMdict gives its source as Dutch \emph{kan}, or English \emph{can}. Its kanji, a character for an earthen jar, is marked as ateji, chosen for its sound.
